name: Sharded ZSETs & Score-Range Histogram Ranking
tagline: Scale real-time rankings past single-node Redis limits by sharding ZSETs by userId % K, merging Top-K via Min-Heap, and serving O(1) ranks via Score Histograms.
purpose: Sustain 200,000+ score updates/sec and sub-15ms p99 Top-K and rank queries across 100M+ active players without single-node RAM or CPU saturation.

spark.summary: Partitioning players across K Redis ZSET shards by userId % K scales write throughput linearly, while a Min-Heap merges global Top-K slices in O(K * T log K) and Score-Range Histograms answer getRank(userId) in O(1).
spark.keyTakeaway: When traffic spikes expose hidden coupling, never funnel 100M-player writes into a single Redis ZSET; shard by userId % K for uniform write scaling and decouple global Top-K and rank reads.
spark.byteSummary:
Core Mechanics & Why Single-Node ZSETs Hit a Wall: A single Redis ZSET holding 100M players consumes 12–16 GB of RAM and saturates Redis's single-threaded event loop at ~100k ZADD/sec—dropping 50% of writes during 200k/sec tournament peaks. Relational SQL ORDER BY queries degrade even faster into O(N log N) sorts.

K-Sharded ZSETs + Min-Heap Merge: Partitioning by userId % K (e.g., K = 16 shards) spreads writes uniformly to 12,500 ZADD/sec and ~6.25M entries per shard. To serve getTopK(T = 100), a coordinator runs parallel ZREVRANGE 0 99 calls across all K shards and merges the K sorted lists with a T-element Min-Heap in O(K * T log K) time, fronted by a 500 ms read-through cache.

O(1) Rank Queries via Score-Range Histograms: Because sharding by userId splits scores across all K nodes, ZREVRANK on one shard no longer gives global rank. Maintaining a Score-Range Histogram (atomic bucket counters per score band plus a prefix-sum array) computes global rank in O(1) time without scanning all K shards.

learningJourney.title: Single-Node Bottlenecks: SQL Sorts & Single-Thread Redis ZSETs
learningJourney.purpose: Quantify why 100M entries and 200k ZADD/sec overwhelm both relational indexes and a single Redis instance.

explanation.foundation: Think of **Single-Node Bottlenecks: SQL Sorts & Single-Thread Redis ZSETs** as the intuition layer for Sharded ZSETs & Score-Range Histogram Ranking: Quantify why 100M entries and 200k ZADD/sec overwhelm both relational indexes and a single Redis instance.
explanation.core: In PostgreSQL, `SELECT COUNT(*) + 1 FROM leaderboard WHERE score > ?` triggers an O(N) index scan at 100M rows. Moving to a single Redis ZSET (skip list + hash table) speeds up individual ops to O(log N), but 100M members burn ~12–16 GB RAM and Redis's single-threaded command loop caps out near ~100k ZADD/sec.
explanation.deepDive: Under heavy load or partial failure, single-node bottlenecks: sql sorts & single-thread redis zsets becomes a critical lever for predictable latency and correctness. Production 100M-player leaderboards add 53-bit composite tie-break encoding, Kafka WAL durability, UNLINK season resets, and stale-while-revalidate fallbacks.

learningJourney.title: Hash Sharding by userId % K for Linear Write Scaling
learningJourney.purpose: Distribute 100M players and 200k ZADD/sec evenly across K = 16 independent Redis shards.

explanation.foundation: Think of **Hash Sharding by userId % K for Linear Write Scaling** as the intuition layer for Sharded ZSETs & Score-Range Histogram Ranking: Distribute 100M players and 200k ZADD/sec evenly across K = 16 independent Redis shards.
explanation.core: Routing `ZADD leaderboard:{userId % 16} score userId` splits 100M users into 6.25M users/shard (~1 GB RAM/shard) and 12,500 writes/sec/shard (~12% of single-node capacity). Because `userId` is uniform, no single shard suffers hot-key skew even when top players battle for #1.

decisionFramework.problem: How to implement Sharded ZSETs & Score-Range Histogram Ranking without hitting unbounded tail latency, state divergence, or operational fragility.
decisionFramework.naiveSolution: Use a single unpartitioned path with unbounded retries and synchronous global coordination.
decisionFramework.whyItFails: Global coordination serializes throughput under load, while unbounded retries amplify transient stalls into full outages.
decisionFramework.alternatives: Compare synchronous strict-consistency paths against bounded asynchronous replication, local caching, or partitioned ownership.
decisionFramework.decision: When traffic spikes expose hidden coupling, never funnel 100M-player writes into a single Redis ZSET; shard by userId % K for uniform write scaling and decouple global Top-K and rank reads.
decisionFramework.tradeOffs: Gains predictable p99 latency and fault isolation in exchange for explicit bounding, observability, and slightly higher implementation complexity.

learningJourney.title: Parallel Scatter-Gather + Min-Heap Top-K Merge
learningJourney.purpose: Reconstruct the exact global Top-T (e.g., Top-100) across K shards in O(K * T log K) time.

explanation.foundation: Because the global Top-100 must be a subset of the union of each shard's local Top-100, the API queries `ZREVRANGE 0 99 WITHSCORES` on all 16 shards in parallel (~2–5 ms) and merges the 16 sorted lists using a k-way merge (`heapq.merge`).

cards.label: 500ms Cache Shield
cards.detail: Caching global Top-100 for 500ms cuts scatter-gather QPS from 100k/s to 2 QPS.

cards.label: Exactness Guarantee
cards.detail: No player outside every shard's local Top-T can ever appear in the global Top-T.

learningJourney.title: Score-Range Prefix Histograms for O(1) Global Rank
learningJourney.purpose: Answer getRank(userId) in O(1) without running K-way ZCOUNT scatter-gathers on every request.

explanation.foundation: If a user is at rank #4,512,300, you cannot use Top-K merge.
explanation.core: Instead, maintain a **Score-Range Histogram** dividing the score space into `B` buckets (e.g., `[0..999]`, `[1000..1999]`, ..., or log-spaced buckets). When a player's score moves from bucket `old_b` to `new_b`, decrement `old_b` and increment `new_b` asynchronously.
explanation.deepDive: Summing counts of buckets strictly above the player's bucket gives an instant O(1) global rank!

cards.label: Exact Inside Top-K
cards.detail: Top 10,000 players use exact ZSET merge; ranks 10k..100M use histogram prefix sums.

cards.label: Adaptive Buckets
cards.detail: Use narrower buckets in dense score bands (e.g., 1,000–2,000 Elo) to keep error < 0.1%.

learningJourney.title: Tie-Breaking & Score Encoding in IEEE-754 Doubles
learningJourney.purpose: Ensure deterministic ranking when two players share the same integer score without overflowing Redis's 53-bit mantissa.

explanation.foundation: Think of **Tie-Breaking & Score Encoding in IEEE-754 Doubles** as the intuition layer for Sharded ZSETs & Score-Range Histogram Ranking: Ensure deterministic ranking when two players share the same integer score without overflowing Redis's 53-bit mantissa.
explanation.core: Redis ZSET scores are IEEE-754 64-bit floats (53 bits of exact integer precision = `9e15`). To break ties by earliest achievement time, pack `(score << 20) | ((MAX_TS - relative_ts) & 0xFFFFF)` as long as total bits stay `<= 53`, or store a secondary tie-break key.
explanation.deepDive: Under heavy load or partial failure, tie-breaking & score encoding in ieee-754 doubles becomes a critical lever for predictable latency and correctness. Production 100M-player leaderboards add 53-bit composite tie-break encoding, Kafka WAL durability, UNLINK season resets, and stale-while-revalidate fallbacks.

cards.label: 53-Bit Ceiling
cards.detail: Exceeding 2^53 causes silent rounding in Redis ZSETs, breaking tie-order.

cards.label: Lexicographical Alternative
cards.detail: If scores exceed 32 bits, use ZADD with score=0 and lexicographical member strings.

learningJourney.title: Durability: Write-Behind WAL & Cold-Start Rebuild
learningJourney.purpose: Recover a lost Redis shard in seconds without losing player scores.

explanation.foundation: Redis is an in-memory serving layer.
explanation.core: Every score update is first appended to a durable Kafka topic / PostgreSQL ledger (partitioned by `userId`), and asynchronously applied to Redis.
explanation.deepDive: If Shard 7 crashes and loses RAM, a warm replica promotes immediately or a recovery job streams Shard 7's Kafka/DB partition to rebuild the ZSET.

cards.label: Idempotent Updates
cards.detail: Prefer absolute ZADD score over ZINCRBY delta, or include monotonic event_id dedup.

cards.label: Zero RDB Stalls
cards.detail: Offload persistence to Kafka/DB so Redis never forks huge 10 GB RDB snapshots on primary.

learningJourney.title: Tournament Reset, Hot-Shard Isolation & Partial Degradation
learningJourney.purpose: Handle seasonal leaderboard resets and single-shard timeouts gracefully.

explanation.foundation: Think of **Tournament Reset, Hot-Shard Isolation & Partial Degradation** as the intuition layer for Sharded ZSETs & Score-Range Histogram Ranking: Handle seasonal leaderboard resets and single-shard timeouts gracefully.
explanation.core: Never run `DEL` on a 6M-entry ZSET synchronously (it blocks Redis for seconds); use `UNLINK` or dual-key season suffixes (`lb:season_42:shard_0`). During `getTopK(100)`, set a 10 ms per-shard timeout—if 1 of 16 shards is slow, serve the cached Top-100 (`stale-while-revalidate`) rather than failing the whole API.
explanation.deepDive: Under heavy load or partial failure, tournament reset, hot-shard isolation & partial degradation becomes a critical lever for predictable latency and correctness. Production 100M-player leaderboards add 53-bit composite tie-break encoding, Kafka WAL durability, UNLINK season resets, and stale-while-revalidate fallbacks.

knowledgeChecks.question: Why should a 100M-player distributed leaderboard shard Redis ZSETs by `userId % K` rather than by score range?

options.text: Redis ZSETs cannot sort negative scores.
options.feedback: Incorrect: Redis ZSETs support arbitrary signed IEEE-754 floats.

options.text: Score-range sharding concentrates all active high-tier players onto one hot shard, whereas userId % K distributes writes uniformly.
options.feedback: Correct: Hash sharding by userId spreads 200k ZADD/s evenly across all K shards without score hot-spots.

options.text: userId % K eliminates the need to merge Top-K.
options.feedback: Incorrect: userId % K requires a scatter-gather Min-Heap merge for global Top-K.
Incorrect: Total RAM is similar; the fatal flaw of score-range sharding is write hot-spotting.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Sharding by userId % K prevents active high-scoring players from creating a write hot-spot on a single score-range shard.

knowledgeChecks.question: When using K = 16 ZSET shards partitioned by `userId % K`, how do you serve `getTopK(100)` without scanning all 100M players?

options.feedback: Incorrect: Global top players are spread across all 16 shards.
Incorrect: Sorting 100M rows in SQL takes seconds and violates the 20ms SLO.

options.text: Fetch each shard's local Top-100 in parallel, merge them with a Min-Heap in O(K * T log K) time, and cache the result for ~500 ms.
options.feedback: Correct: The global Top-100 is guaranteed to come from the union of the 16 local Top-100 lists.
Incorrect: HyperLogLog counts distincts, not ordered Top-K scores.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Parallel ZREVRANGE 0 99 across K shards plus a Min-Heap merge computes exact global Top-100 in O(K * T log K) time.

knowledgeChecks.question: Why is a Score-Range Prefix Histogram used for `getRank(userId)` on a K-sharded leaderboard?

options.text: It lets you compute a player's global rank in O(1) time via bucket prefix sums without issuing K-way ZCOUNT queries per read.
options.feedback: Correct: Prefix sums over score-range buckets turn global rank lookups into O(1) reads.

options.text: Because Redis ZSETs do not have a ZREVRANK command.
options.feedback: Incorrect: Redis has ZREVRANK, but on a sharded ZSET it only returns local shard rank.
Incorrect: Histograms are for fast rank reads, not write durability.
Incorrect: Tie-breaking uses composite 53-bit scores; histograms accelerate global rank queries.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Because ZREVRANK only knows local shard rank, a Score-Range Prefix Histogram enables O(1) global rank lookups.
